title: Checking photos, videos and voices
essentialQuestion: How can you check a photo, video or voice before you trust it?
learningGoal: Explain how AI can make realistic pictures, videos and voices, tell labelled creative work from a fake, and check the source before you trust or share one.

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: Who posted each one? What does the source tell you? Which post says openly that AI made it?

cards.title: Posts in the Greenhill news group

cases.name: Post A: a giant pumpkin
cases.body: A photo of a pumpkin as big as a car, posted by a page with no name. The Greenhill farm's own page says it grew no giant pumpkin this year. The farmer's hand in the photo looks a little odd.

cases.name: Post B: a talking goat
cases.body: A video of a goat that says “Good morning” in clear words. The Greenhill comedy club posted it. The caption says: “Made with AI, just for fun.”

cases.name: Post C: a voice message
cases.body: A voice message that sounds like Coach Ana. It says: “The football game moves to six in the morning.” It came from a number nobody knows. The notice board at the centre still says four in the afternoon.

cases.name: Post D: a fruit seller
cases.body: A photo of a fruit seller. Her skin looks very smooth, and the background is blurry. The Greenhill photo club posted it with the photographer's name, and says it was taken with a phone in the evening.

sections.heading: AI can make pictures, videos and voices
sections.text: Some AI tools can create new pictures, videos and voices. These tools learned from enormous numbers of real examples, so what they make can look and sound realistic. Many people use these tools openly and creatively. Artists make pictures, film makers add effects and teachers make lessons, and they say that AI helped. In Greenhill, the comedy club posted a talking goat with the label “Made with AI, just for fun”, so that is not a trick. A fake is different: it pretends to show something real that never happened. A deepfake is a fake that copies a real person's face or voice, often to trick people for money or attention. Labels can get lost, too. If someone shares the goat video without its label, as if it were real, it can mislead people.
sections.simpler: Some AI tools make new pictures, videos and voices. They learned from lots of real examples. So the new ones look realistic. Many people use these tools openly. Artists, film makers and teachers say when AI helped. In Greenhill, the comedy club posted a talking goat. Its label says AI made it, just for fun. That is not a trick. A fake is different. It shows something that never happened, as if it were real. A deepfake copies a real person's face or voice to trick people. Labels can get lost too. Shared without its label, the goat video could fool people.

sections.heading: Strange details are clues, not proof
sections.text: AI pictures sometimes have small mistakes, such as an extra finger, messy letters on a sign or a background that melts into a wall. In a video, the mouth may not move with the words. These details can be clues, but they are not proof. Newer tools make fewer mistakes, so a fake can look perfect. Real photographs can also look strange, for example when they are blurry or taken in poor light. In a 2025 study by researchers in the United States, more than 50,000 people judged real photos and AI pictures online. They wrongly called about one in four real photos AI-made, and they also missed about one in four AI pictures. The fruit seller's photo has very smooth skin, but the photo club says who took it, with a phone.
sections.simpler: AI pictures sometimes have mistakes, like six fingers or messy letters. These are clues. But clues are not proof. New tools make fewer mistakes. Real photos can look strange too, when they are dark or not sharp. In a 2025 study, more than 50,000 people looked at pictures online. Some were real, and some were AI. People called about one in four real photos AI-made. They also missed about one in four AI pictures. The fruit seller has very smooth skin. But the photo club says a phone took it.

sections.heading: Check the source
sections.text: So the most useful check is the source. Who posted it, and when? Can you find where it first came from, and does the maker say how it was made? Do other trusted sources show the same thing? Make sure they did not all copy one post, because ten copies are still one source. Fact-checking groups do this work for pictures that spread widely. In Greenhill, the farm's own page says it grew no giant pumpkin, and a page with no name posted the photo. So that photo is probably fake. For a voice message, contact the person in another way. Coach Ana's message came from an unknown number, so ask her in person. If you still can't tell, say so, and don't share it yet.
sections.simpler: So check the source. Who posted it? When? Where did it come from first? Do people you trust show the same thing? Check that they did not just copy one post. The farm says it grew no giant pumpkin. A page with no name posted the photo. So it is probably fake. Coach Ana's message came from a number nobody knows. So ask her in person. Not sure? Say so, and don't share it yet.

glossary.definition: Looking or sounding like the real thing.
glossary.example: The goat video looks realistic, but its label says AI made it.

glossary.definition: Made to look real, but it is not real.
glossary.example: The pumpkin photo is probably a fake.

glossary.definition: A fake picture, video or voice that copies a real person, made with AI.
glossary.example: A deepfake of Coach Ana's voice could trick the football team.

glossary.definition: A small sign that helps you find out something.
glossary.example: An extra finger is a clue to check a picture. It is not proof.

glossary.definition: The person or place that information comes from.
glossary.example: The farm's own page is a good source about its pumpkins.

checks.question: What is the strongest reason to doubt the giant pumpkin photo?

options.text: The farmer's hand in the photo looks a bit odd
options.feedback: Not quite. An odd hand is a reason to check, not proof. Real photos can look odd too. Read the second section.

options.text: The farm says it grew no giant pumpkin
options.feedback: Yes. The farm is the best source about its own pumpkins, and the page that posted the photo has no name.

options.text: The pumpkin is a very bright orange
options.feedback: Not quite. Real pumpkins are orange too. Read about checking the source in the third section.

checks.question: The comedy club's goat video says “Made with AI, just for fun”. Is it a fake?

options.feedback: Not quite. AI made it, but the club says so openly. A fake pretends to be real. Read the first section.
Not quite. Nobody is meant to believe it. It is a labelled joke. Read the first section.

options.text: No, because it says that AI made it
options.feedback: Yes. Labelled creative work is not a trick. It could mislead people if someone shared it without the label.

write.prompt: Explain how a labelled AI video is different from a fake. Use the Greenhill posts. Then say how you would check a surprising picture before you share it.
sentenceStarters: The goat video is not a fake because ...
Before I share a surprising picture, I would check ...
write.example: The goat video is not a fake because the comedy club says openly that AI made it, just for fun. Nobody is meant to believe a goat can talk. A fake is different because it pretends to show something real. The giant pumpkin photo came from a page with no name, and the farm says it grew no giant pumpkin. Before I share a surprising picture, I would check who posted it and where it first came from. I would also look for trusted sources that show the same thing.

speak.partnerTask: Your partner plays a teammate who got the Coach Ana voice message and wants to tell everyone. Explain how to check it first. Then switch: your partner explains why the goat video is not a fake.
speak.independentTask: Say out loud why a strange detail in a picture is a clue, not proof. Then say two better ways to check where it came from.

watch.title: AI Unlocked: Recognizing AI-generated content
watch.why: It was made with teenage fact-checkers, and it shows the clues in AI-made pictures, videos and voices.
watch.beforeQuestion: What do you think a fake video might get wrong?
watch.afterQuestion: Why is it not enough to trust a tool that says if something is fake?
watch.summary: This video comes from a series made with a team of teenage fact-checkers. It explains that some people use AI to make fake pictures, videos and sounds. They often do it to get money, attention or power. The video shows clues to look for. AI pictures can have strange hands, odd shadows and strange backgrounds. In AI videos, look for edges that blur or flicker. Check the shadows, and check if the lips move with the words. For AI voices, listen to the tone and to the sounds in the background. The video also shows tools that can help, like a search that finds where else a picture appears online. But these tools are not always right. A person still needs to think and check before sharing.
keyPoints: AI fakes can have clues: odd hands, shadows, backgrounds, edges or lips.
For a voice, listen to the tone and the background sounds.
Tools that spot fakes are not always right, so a person still needs to check.
watch.contentNote: Fast American English with real examples of AI-made content. It mentions tools that need the internet (reverse image search and AI detection apps); on an offline device, learners can ask a teacher instead. The summary was written from PBS NewsHour Classroom's lesson plan for this video, not from watching it. The video teaches visual clues; the lesson treats them as reasons to check, never proof. Preview it first; learners can read the written summary instead.

sensitiveNotes: Deepfakes are used to hurt real people: fake pictures that shame someone, fake videos of leaders, and cloned voices in scams (for example a call that sounds like a relative asking for money; see the FTC source). The lesson keeps its examples silly on purpose. Don't show real deepfakes of real people in class. If a learner says a fake was made of them or someone they know, don't discuss the details in class; follow the partner's own safeguarding process.
educatorNotes: Teach checking first: who posted it, when, where it first came from, whether the maker says how it was made, whether other trusted sources show the same thing (and didn't all copy one post), and for a voice, contacting the person another way. Visual glitches (extra fingers, messy letters, smooth skin) are reasons to check, never proof: newer tools make fewer of them, and real photos can show odd details too. The study in section 2 is Kamali and others (CHI '25, Northwestern University): more than 50,000 online participants judged 450 AI-made and 149 real images; they called real photographs real in 74% of observations and AI-made images AI-made in 76%, so about one in four was misjudged each way. It is one online study with the authors' own image set, not a general rate. Accept “can't tell yet” as a strong answer. On paper, read the four Greenhill posts aloud and discuss what each source tells you; there is no sorting task.

Labelled AI work (art, film effects, lessons, a joke clearly marked “Made with AI”) is not the same as a fake that pretends to be real or copies a real person. Labels can be lost when a picture is reposted (News Literacy Project, 2026), so a labelled post can become misleading when shared without it. In Indonesia, Mafindo's TurnBackHoax and CekFakta check viral pictures and videos, and Mafindo says AI-based hoaxes are getting harder to tell apart (Liputan6, 2026). A teacher with internet can show one checked example; learners don't need to go online.

October 2026, social studies rebuild (Justin's brief: AI and the digital world through a social studies lens, at most 20 lessons): kept as Lesson 13 in "Truth, power and choices" (truth-and-power). The notes above about the old section ids are out of date.

Revised on 1 November 2026 from Justin's review: checking the source is now the core skill (who posted it, when, where it first came from, who else shows it, and asking the person another way for a voice); visual glitches are taught as clues to check, never proof, with a dated study showing people call about one in four real photos AI-made (Kamali and others, CHI '25), and the evidence, activity, quick check, Write example and Speak no longer reward spotting fingers or skin. A new group, “Made with AI, and it says so”, separates labelled creative work (the comedy club's goat) from deceptive fakes and deepfakes; Post F is now a real photo that only looks odd. Feedback gives the reason, not “what most people would say”. The evidence stays fully fictional; the real study is in the reading, the teacher notes and sources (the News Literacy Project lesson plan and MIT Detect Fakes sources were replaced by sources opened for this revision). Title unchanged; “Checking photos, videos and voices” would fit the lesson better (for Nick and Justin to decide).

Revised on 8 November 2026 (Justin's brief of 4 November): the sort activity, the warm-up, the think question, the planning boxes and the self-check are gone, and the evidence is down to four posts (the rain and cat posts existed only for sorting). The reading teaches more: open, creative uses of AI-made media set against deception, and how a label is lost when a post is reshared without it; the 2025 study now reports both errors (about one in four real photos called AI-made, about one in four AI pictures missed); the source check adds where a post first came from and that agreeing sources may all have copied one post.

Write is one explanation (labelled work against a fake, and how to check); the quick check keeps two questions, on the source and on labelled work; Speak is a role play about the voice message. estimatedMinutes 25–40.
